audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet final Jerusalem siege, Zedekiah capture and blinding, temple and city destruction, executions and exile, Gedaliah governorship and assassination, flight to Egypt, and Jehoiachin release narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for siege chronology, famine, military flight, Zedekiah's capture, killing of his sons before him, blinding and restraints, urban and temple burning, wall destruction, mass deportation, poor agricultural laborers left, cultural extraction, Riblah executions, colonial governorship, political assassination, refugee flight to Egypt, and Jehoiachin's limited elevation in Babylon.

verses.restored: In ninth year of his reign, in tenth month, on tenth of month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem. He camped against it and built siege works around it.

familiar.text: And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about.

modern.text: So in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army. They encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it.

familiar.text: And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, there came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Careah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men.

modern.text: When all the commanders of the armies and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor, they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah—Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, as well as their men.

original.text: וַיִּשְׁמְעוּ֩ כָל שָׂרֵ֨י הַחֲיָלִ֜ים הֵ֣מָּה וְהָאֲנָשִׁ֗ים כִּֽי הִפְקִ֤יד מֶֽלֶךְ בָּבֶל֙ אֶת גְּדַלְיָ֔הוּ וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ אֶל גְּדַלְיָ֖הוּ הַמִּצְפָּ֑ה וְיִשְׁמָעֵ֣אל בֶּן נְתַנְיָ֡ה וְיוֹחָנָ֣ן בֶּן קָ֠רֵחַ וּשְׂרָיָ֨ה בֶן תַּנְחֻ֜מֶת הַנְּטֹפָתִ֗י וְיַֽאֲזַנְיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן הַמַּ֣עֲכָתִ֔י הֵ֖מָּה וְאַנְשֵׁיהֶֽם

verses.restored: Gedaliah swore to them and their men and said to them, Do not fear servants of Chaldeans. Live in land, serve king of Babylon, and it will be well for you.

familiar.text: And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you.

modern.text: And Gedaliah took an oath before them and their men, assuring them, “Do not be afraid of the servants of the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.” The Murder of Gedaliah (Jeremiah 41:1–10)

original.text: וַיִּשָּׁבַ֨ע לָהֶ֤ם גְּדַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ וּלְאַנְשֵׁיהֶ֔ם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם אַל תִּֽירְא֖וּ מֵעַבְדֵ֣י הַכַּשְׂדִּ֑ים שְׁב֣וּ בָאָ֗רֶץ וְעִבְד֛וּ אֶת מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל וְיִטַ֥ב לָכֶֽם

verses.restored: In seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elishama, from royal seed, came, and ten men with him. They struck Gedaliah, and he died, along with Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.

familiar.text: But it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, came, and ten men with him, and smote Gedaliah, that he died, and the Jews and the Chaldees that were with him at Mizpah.

modern.text: In the seventh month, however, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, who was a member of the royal family, came with ten men and struck down and killed Gedaliah, along with the Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.

original.text: וַיְהִ֣י בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י בָּ֣א יִשְׁמָעֵ֣אל בֶּן נְ֠תַנְיָה בֶּן אֱלִ֨ישָׁמָ֜ע מִזֶּ֣רַע הַמְּלוּכָ֗ה וַעֲשָׂרָ֤ה אֲנָשִׁים֙ אִתּ֔וֹ וַיַּכּ֥וּ אֶת גְּדַלְיָ֖הוּ וַיָּמֹ֑ת וְאֶת הַיְּהוּדִים֙ וְאֶת הַכַּשְׂדִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁר הָי֥וּ אִתּ֖וֹ בַּמִּצְפָּֽה

verses.restored: All people, from small to great, and commanders of armies arose and came to Egypt, for they feared Chaldeans.

familiar.text: And all the people, both small and great, and the captains of the armies, arose, and came to Egypt: for they were afraid of the Chaldees.

modern.text: Then all the people small and great, together with the commanders of the army, arose and fled to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans. Jehoiachin Released from Prison (Jeremiah 52:31–34)

original.text: וַיָּקֻ֨מוּ כָל הָעָ֜ם מִקָּטֹ֤ן וְעַד גָּדוֹל֙ וְשָׂרֵ֣י הַחֲיָלִ֔ים וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ מִצְרָ֑יִם כִּ֥י יָרְא֖וּ מִפְּנֵ֥י כַשְׂדִּֽים

verses.restored: In thirty-seventh year of exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in twelfth month, on twenty-seventh of month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in year he became king, lifted head of Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison.

familiar.text: And it came to pass in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the year that he began to reign did lift up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison;

modern.text: On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Judah’s King Jehoiachin, in the year Evil-merodach became king of Babylon, he released King Jehoiachin of Judah from prison.

original.text: וַיְהִי֩ בִשְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וָשֶׁ֜בַע שָׁנָ֗ה לְגָלוּת֙ יְהוֹיָכִ֣ין מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה בִּשְׁנֵ֤ים עָשָׂר֙ חֹ֔דֶשׁ בְּעֶשְׂרִ֥ים וְשִׁבְעָ֖ה לַחֹ֑דֶשׁ נָשָׂ֡א אֱוִ֣יל מְרֹדַךְ֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ בָּבֶ֜ל בִּשְׁנַ֣ת מָלְכ֗וֹ אֶת רֹ֛אשׁ יְהוֹיָכִ֥ין מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֖ה מִבֵּ֥ית כֶּֽלֶא

verses.restored: He spoke good things with him and set his throne above thrones of kings who were with him in Babylon.

familiar.text: And he spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon;

modern.text: And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.

original.text: וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ טֹב֑וֹת וַיִּתֵּן֙ אֶת כִּסְא֔וֹ מֵעַ֗ל כִּסֵּ֧א הַמְּלָכִ֛ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בְּבָבֶֽל

verses.restored: He changed garments of his imprisonment, and Jehoiachin ate bread continually before him all days of his life.

familiar.text: And changed his prison garments: and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life.

modern.text: So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life.

original.text: וְשִׁנָּ֕א אֵ֖ת בִּגְדֵ֣י כִלְא֑וֹ וְאָכַ֨ל לֶ֧חֶם תָּמִ֛יד לְפָנָ֖יו כָּל יְמֵ֥י חַיָּֽיו

verses.restored: His allowance was a continual allowance given to him from king, a day's portion in its day, all days of his life.

familiar.text: And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.

modern.text: And the king provided Jehoiachin a daily portion for the rest of his life.

original.text: וַאֲרֻחָת֗וֹ אֲרֻחַ֨ת תָּמִ֧יד נִתְּנָה לּ֛וֹ מֵאֵ֥ת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ דְּבַר י֣וֹם בְּיוֹמ֑וֹ כֹּ֖ל יְמֵ֥י חַיָּֽו

translation_notes: The siege lasts into a devastating famine. Starvation is a weapon and consequence of war, not proof that hungry civilians lacked faith or deserved suffering.
Zedekiah's sons are killed before his eyes, then he is blinded and restrained. This is torture designed to combine bereavement, sensory injury, humiliation, and captivity.
Blindness and disability are not the shame in verse 7; deliberate mutilation and imperial cruelty are. Disabled people must never be used as symbols of moral blindness or ruined masculinity.
Burning temple, palace, and homes and destroying city walls are cultural, religious, domestic, and civic devastation—not merely fulfillment or architectural change.
Those left as vineyard and field workers are called poorest of land. They retain full dignity and become coerced survivors responsible for food production amid destroyed institutions.
Temple bronze and vessels are dismantled and transferred. Material detail preserves the scale of cultural extraction and the loss of collective craft heritage.
Priests, officials, military personnel, a scribe, and sixty people are transported to Riblah and executed. Captive killing without due process remains atrocity.
Gedaliah governs under Babylonian appointment. His advice may be pragmatic survival under occupation, not free political consent or endorsement of empire.
Ishmael's royal descent does not legitimate assassination. His killing of Gedaliah, Judeans, and Chaldeans destabilizes the surviving community.
The flight to Egypt is refugee movement caused by credible fear of imperial reprisal. Displaced people must not be condemned for seeking safety.
Jehoiachin's release, changed clothing, table access, and daily allowance improve one prisoner's conditions but do not end exile, empire, dependence, or the suffering of the wider community.
Kings, Jeremiah, Chronicles, Ezekiel, and Babylonian evidence contain chronological and numerical differences requiring source-witness audit.
safety_note: Do not romanticize siege, starvation, child killing, blinding, cultural destruction, captive execution, occupation, assassination, or exile. Do not stigmatize disability or poverty, and do not condemn refugees who flee to Egypt. The book ends with limited dignity restored to one prisoner—not with empire defeated or collective trauma resolved.
